blocks.x: What's that? Johnny Gould, the first string band ever, you know, ragtime band ever heard. Then afterwards they come with the mother band, the Cucked Seeders and the string band with Manuel Perez and this fellow, Naum Manetta, one of them fellows that's in the old, that's before your time. So Naum Manetta, I bought his horn after he died. That was Manuel Manetta's uncle. Yeah, here it's been a long time. Oh yeah? Yeah, it's been a long time. I bought his horn.
Was that the first horn you ever had?

That's the first horn I ever bought. You see the first time I started to play it was the ghetto. I played ghetto a while and it was too slow and I went and bought a violin. And I went to Jimmy, take a lesson with Jimmy, we used to call him Jimmy Sprig, but he named Jimmy Pallard. Well I take a lesson with him. He used to take a lesson with the professor before those French Opry went down. You know, we used to have a French Opry here right on Toulouse Street there. You don't remember that. No, but I was saying he took this over. Yeah. Well that old professor was playing, then Jimmy used to come over and take a lesson with him. I believe he was paying him a dollar and half a lesson and I was paying him 75 cents. When he take this lesson, I'll go to, you need to come over and he give me my lesson. You understand? That's what caused me to start to play music. Yeah. But I started to take a lesson with my hand before I started to play it violin. Then I played violin a long time, lead to playing a long time with the violin. And that got too slow and I picked up the connet myself.
Business was slow on those instruments?
Yeah, on them instruments. Yeah. And I picked up the connet myself. No violin didn't show me nothing about no connet.
Well who was that professor in the French opera? Do you remember his name?
No, I don't know. Old French.
Old French. Ever hear about Professor James Follett or Jimmy Follett? No.
I don't know his name. I don't know his name. I see. Wasn't bad.
Oh, how did you learn guitar?
Well I just learned it, picked it up, learned it.

Yeah, I didn't take a lesson. I just would go around and play it in guitar. I don't play in no band, just around the streets you understand? Oh I see. Yes. Then I take the violin, then I start to play it in the band, lead the band. That got too slow and I picked up the connet. I see. I just bought a connet from Naumanela. Nobody gave me a lesson but I know the music. After I got that I just bought the music, I know the music and I just went on. Nobody had learned it and teach me no connet. How did you learn how to tune a guitar? Did anybody ever show you that? Well I listened to the other fellow. Oh, who'd you listen to? Yeah, Albert Mitchell. Oh yeah, I see. Yeah. the violin. Yeah, he just tuned up and get, I just ended up violin. I seen tuning up a violin. And I just could stand up and sit on and just let you tune up. I can tune up a violin. I can tune up a violin. Mm-hm. I had to tune up to the violin.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. I don't know, because I had the tone. I had the tone. I could tune up without nobody, you know, and I'll tell you whether to tune up or not. You see I had the tone in my head.
Right in your ear.

Yeah, right in your ear. And violin too? Yeah, when your legs that you know your tone gets down, you don't forget it. You just pick it up. I can get it from string to string and tune it up before I fake it.
Yeah. Well what kind of guitar did you play? Did you play with a pick or with your fingers or both?
With a little, when I used to play a guitar, I used to pick.
Pick with your fingers?
With my fingers, yeah. When you're playing in the band you have a little piece of, you know, you should sing, but I know the band. I only just pick, it was a pick of guitar.
And what would you play on the guitar? Oh, just play every little thing.

A little tune. Yeah, a choice hand or something like that. Yeah, it was a little thing I used to play. But I never played in a band then when I had the guitar. When it got too slow and I got a violin, then I went and made a band of myself. You understand?
How many fingers do you use when you pick a guitar?
A guitar, some use one, but I used to use them all. Use them all?
Yeah.
I used to use all of my fingers but some of them pick with one finger. But I used to use them all.
Well can you play second with your thumb or? Yeah, well. You could second with your thumb or?
Yeah, well.
You could second with your thumb or stuff?

Yeah, I could second with my thumb and use them all. I used to pick with all of my fingers. Oh yeah. Yeah. Yeah. But some of them pick with one. Yeah. And use a second with the thumb. Yeah. But I used to pick with all of my fingers. I don't know why I was right at all but I just picked it up myself.
What was the first tune you ever learned on the guitar?
Well, I don't know myself. It was a little thing, you know, anything I was young that I played, you know.
Well what kind of music were people playing in those days?

Well, right kind, just any little thing you hear. Yeah. Any little thing you hear, the other fellow play, you catch that. He wasn't playing no, he wasn't with the orchestration music, he wouldn't stand about that. You see? He used to call it parlor music. I used to go to play, there was a fish fry, they said don't play that, put the notes down. They didn't want the notes. You know what I'm saying? They called it parlor music in them times. They wanted the redhead music. And then the little thing you hear. You see? You sing a song, you catch that song and go play. You see? That's what we used to play. Now me, I know it was rag time, you know, I always played music. But they used to call me parlor music. And then when the time there was, the music time comes and everybody had to read, they You understand? I had to show them different things. Yeah, the division and everything like that. You see I learned that before I picked up my horn, you see. When I first started playing violin, when I learned about, I stayed about almost a month or two or three months before the division. You don't know the division, you just want to start playing music. You see, you got to know the division. Know the notes, half notes, whole notes, sixty-fold, thirty-second, you have to know all that, you understand, before. Well I know that. That's why I learned the horn. You see I didn't have to go, all I wanted to know was the scale. Well I could pick up any kind of instrument, because I know the music, just get the music and I could play, you see. I only want to know the scale. After you get the scale and the thing, well you know when you make A, you know when you make C, D, that's all you want to know. Well the music is right there, but you see that made it easy for me. Nobody didn't learn me to know a cornet. I learned it myself, you see, because I know the music. And I bought me a method, a cornet method, so I just went right on. I know the division. I played with Ullett, once or twice. You heard of anybody, Ullett? No. Old professor?
No.

Old professor Ullett. He was one of the owners, one of the years used to play violin. I called him Ullett. I played with them. Cantrell used to play drums, a fellow called Cantrell, used to play drums with him. But I know his son.
Yeah.
His son is a clarinet player.
Yeah. I don't know his son, no.
I know him. Well you all lived where? What part of town was you? Well in the French part of the town, yeah, downtown there. Yeah.
But he was an old professor. Yeah.

And this boy there, his father, I went to the school, and I went to the school, and I picked up clarinet, but I put it down. I went and took two lessons with Willie Umford, the old man Umford, that's his father. Willie Umford's boys, Percy, Umford, and Willie. He played yesterday or day.
Oh yeah.

I know. Yeah. Well I had taken two lessons with their father on clarinet, but I put it down. On the tiptoe, let's do it with their father. The old man. Yeah. And I played with T.O., all them old professors there, you see, because I know the music. You played with T.O.?
Yeah. I played with T.O.
I played one or two jobs. They had the band, but sometimes the fellow would get on a drunk, they'd come and get me. Well which T.O. was that?
I never can keep them straight. There's three of them I know. Well the old man, old man T.O.
Well they got the father, you know, they got the father and the son playing too.
And you played with which one?
I played with the old man who was playing violin. Yeah. And I played with him, he had a band too. T.O.? T.O. T.O. T.O., yeah.
I thought he was a fireneck player.

Well T.O. wait, let me get this thing straight. T.O. He didn't have the son playing piano. The son played piano? Yeah. And his father used to play, I believe, violin. Oh I see. Yeah. His father used to play violin. T.O. used to play violin. T.O. used to play violin. T.O. T.O. I see. I see. I want to ask you, do you remember the Spanish and American War?
Yeah.
Were you playing music then?
I played guitar then. Spanish and American War.

Of course I left to City Park with him. And they were afraid for raids. They had a ship, they had taken the ship in the Espanade in the river. And the ship they were waiting for him. So I was about 16 years old then. And I was, I watched, I was living in the Nile Jays. And I would come over here just to see him go away, you know, leave. The old Spanish Belt. I was old, I was big enough to join the army, but I was two years. And I marched with him up to the Espanade and the Kera. And I went on the wall for the ship, left the Spanish Belt and the Wall. When the old guy on the ship left that evening about half past six that evening. And I would stand on the wall when they left. Did they have a band?
Yes, they had a band.

Would it be a brass band? They had a brass band, but I didn't know who that band was. Led them from the, from the City Park I think it was. And led them to, they come on Espanade Street, but right on the wall there. It was 30th Street Ferry, and on the side they had a wall there and that's why the ship was there.
Well was that a white band or a colored band or do you know?
A colored band.
Did they mix it up then, the musicians? Did they mix it up, the white and colored musicians there?

Well no, they didn't mix it up. They had some fellas you know, you couldn't tell them from whites, you understand. They used to mix up them. Oh, Emmanuel Meletta had his brother there, used to play in the white band. And there were old man and Ulec. Old man Ulec, he used to play corn at the, used to play in the, I don't forget that band, that's the only big band they had in town here then. Old man Ulec, he was the leader. And now Manela, when I brought the horn, we used to play with him, them times. Well now I went band, went with them people, I was young then, I just didn't know, but I was looking at the Jordan going to the soldiers going to catch the ship. I was about sixty years old then.
What was Fest's brother's name, do you remember?
Well, John, he used to call him John, Fest's brother. John? John, they used to call him. John. John, yeah. John. John. But I don't think he ever played any music, I don't think.
But he could, he was real bright, huh?
Yeah, oh yeah, Creole, yeah. He was real bright. Of course, what do you want to say?
Did you ever see any flagpole raisins with a band? Well, oh yeah, I seen a flagpole raisin.

I was playing in the, in the, uh, Razo, and I was playing out there with the string band, and they was, they had a pot go shooting. A what? Pot go. She had a big thing on the, uh, on a pole. And there was good shots there in the country. That was way in the, uh, Razo, they call it. Razo. I know.
Down near Delacro, on the way to Delacro.

Delacro, yeah. Well, they had a, right over the bayou, they had a pot go shooting, and when they raised up the flag, they had a flag raised in there, before the pot go shooting, well. And then the best shot, you know, split that kind of a boy, the duck, you see, on a post. That's where the flag raised in the army. I see them fellas, uh, you know, at night, uh, in the evening, they, a wheel past, they see them take the flag down.
But you didn't play for that, huh?
No.
No. What's pot go mean?
Eh?
What does pot go mean?
Pot go is a, it's a thing made like a boy.
Oh, yeah.
And they put it on the posts, a big posts. So, so fun, and you use a shotgun.
It's like a decoy.
Like a decoy. That's what it is. And some fellas there, split them in half, and some fellas there can cut them in half.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah. Yeah, see, so he win the prize. He's shooting for a prize.
I see.
Yeah. That's all the flag raised in the army. I saw a lot of flag raised in the Navy and something like that, but none of them, no flag raised.
Well, when you had your jazz band, when you had Kid Alpert's band, how many men in it would take down at once? Well, you know, so you played at once?

Yeah, yeah, at once, well, we always would get on and then you never take down at the blowing instrument. We'd take down. Mm-hmm. Take down one or two bars. Mm-hmm. And they didn't have much singing then. Yeah. Didn't have much singing then. You know, they had a pen of singing then. We'd take down and rest, pick up again. Then the trombone, take down, the clanner, take down and rest a while, you know. Mm-hmm. We got a hard job, something like that, you understand. We'd take down and rest, but no much singing, no singing that time. Yeah. They didn't have no, I played when they didn't have no drums. Mm-hmm. Didn't have no drums when I played with Johnny Gould in there.
Oh, yeah.
They didn't have no drums then. Afterwards, they'd come to get the drums.
Did they have drums when they had the big storm here? When they had the big storm? Did the drums come in by the time of the big storm?
But I think it is, after the storm, I think after the storm the drums come in. And the saxophone, they didn't have no saxophone. Oh, yeah?
Who?
They didn't have no saxophone then. I didn't see them. They was using alto. Mm-hmm. The peck horn.
Yeah.
Use kind of a peck horn. But I never seen no saxophone like, but they used to have the key trombone. They didn't hear the slide.
Well who was the first saxophone man here in town?
Look, I don't know the first saxophone man. I know the slide and trombone they had that was Fess, Fess Uncle. Dude, he used to call him. I don't know, what's his name, Fess Uncle? Deuce, huh?
Deuce, yeah.
Deuce, I think.
We can check with Fess. Yeah.
Well he was the first slide I ever seen playing the slide. And when did that happen? Was that?
Oh, that was, well, it was. Was that before you played music?
That's before I played music, yeah. Oh, no, I was playing violin.
You were playing guitar, or? No, I was playing no violin.
You were playing violin? No, I was playing violin. You were playing violin.
Yeah, I was playing violin. Yeah, playing violin.

Yeah, playing violin. Yeah. He didn't even tie it, but I never did. He used to come over there and play it when I was young, you understand? Mm-hm. Used to be around first. Well I was the first one taking him and Peeta on the job. He used to come over there and play when I was young, you understand? Used to be around the fest. Well I was the first one taking him and Peter on the job. Oh yeah? Fest. They was learning and I'd take them down the breakway in the cane cart. After grinding. I was the first one they played a job with. Fest with. And you know that was a long time. They were little boys. I'd take them down and with me. I was playing the violin. Peter was playing the violin. I'd not get tired. No. Peter was playing the cornet. All of us could play the little cornet. Peter could play the little cornet and Manuel could play it. Fest would play the little cornet. Well I had somebody to help me. My lips used to swell on the uniform. Well I'd take the violin. We'd say you know, I'd take the violin and play. What happened, it didn't swell, we didn't change up, but that's what I'd take them for. They helped me out.
Who else did you have in that band?
Well it had been so long I'd never forgotten them fellas. I had so many of them.
Was it before Skeeter played with you? I'm the guitar player?
I believe I did have Skeeter. I believe Skeeter did play with me then. I think he did. Yeah, he played a while with me too. What was Skeeter's name?
No, I don't know his other name.
There's one that called Skeeter. Yeah, I don't know his other name. Just Skeeter. Yeah. He played a while with me. Uh huh.
Mm-hm. Oh I wanted to ask you, did you ever hear of a guy called Bobo over there from a concert?
Bobo? What did he play? He played ballets. Left hand. Left hand? Yeah. After I started to play ballets, I took his job.
You took his job? Yeah. Oh yeah?

Yeah. What band was that? He had a little band in the Nile Jays. And Edmund Payton used to play in the ghetto. A little fellow, he called him Edmund Payton. That's a long time for him. That's a long time for him. So I take the job. After I got good I take the job for him. Yeah. So that's Bobo. You've got some of this old stuff.
Well I don't know anything about Payton.
Edmund Payton.
I don't know anything about him. I've never heard of him before.
Yeah, Edmund Payton. He used to play ghetto.
Well did he ever play on this side or anywhere?
No, he was playing out of his. Yeah, playing out of his. A little bit of string man they had on the outside. After I got there, I made up of a band. Six pieces. Five pieces. Four pieces.
Well what about Eddie Atkins? Did you ever know him?

Well yeah, he's over here. He used to play a trumpet with Eddie Atkins. Did he ever play with you? No, he played in the brass band. You know, sometimes he used to make up with a band, once or twice. Them fellas, Ed Atkins. But he's playing with different bands in town. Jack Kerrin. That's his brother. That's his brother. He used to play with Jack Kerrin. And I played one of two jobs with Jack Kerrin, too, on the way down around Lutches. Through there on the other side of the road, on the Isaiah side. Yeah, I played with them too, a while with Jack Kerrin. I played a couple of jobs with him. I played with them all. Yeah, in them times. When you go down, say, to Delacroix, did you have to play any special numbers for those people down there? Did they like different numbers? Yes. Yes. Yes. Different numbers we used to play. We used to play sometimes, whether the wings are or not. We used to play some time. We used to play some time. We used to play some time.
Not shy, not shy, but we called it lancers. We used to play lancers at them time. You understand?

We used to play sometimes, well we used to play, not Charters, call it Lancers, but we used to play Lancers at them times. You understand? But they don't play that no more. And mazookas, that's the only thing they used to play down there, mazookas. They like mazookas? They like mazookas down there. And it was rough stuff you know. There was mazookas and Charters, they never did bother with that. Only mazookas, walls, and two steps.
Well that down in Delacroix?
In Delacroix.
Do you remember the names of any of those tunes?
Well, no, just anything. I see.
Well did they like Spanish noppas because they were Spanish men?
Yeah, they used to play, they had a Spanish number, Johnny Gould used to play for them. Yeah.
Do you remember it?
Let me see that again. Well that's La Paloma, isn't it?
Yeah. Yeah, La Paloma.
Yeah, that's it, that's the one I used to play for them.
I see. Yeah. What about them Cajuns?
Them Cajuns?
Did they like any special kind of noppas? What did they like?

Well, Cajuns, anything. Waltz, some of them couldn't dance no mazookas. Most of them islands, Spanish people used to dance mazookas. Them Cajuns used to dance none but wals and two steps, that's all. I know they love waltzes. Oh, waltzes, two steps, that's all. Did you ever sing? And once a slow drag, a little slow drag. Yeah. Yeah. They play a hula, play a note, play it slow. Yeah.
Did anybody ever sing in your band to them and sing in French? No, nobody had to sing in French. When did that La Bar come in then?
Oh. Was that in the late years or was it? That was in the late years, La Bar.
Yeah. Used to sing, that girl used to sing the first time I was going to sing. What's her name? Used to sing there.

She don't sing no more. Sing out here. What's her name? Oh, that Herb Moran sister? Lizzy? What's her name? Lizzy Mao. Yeah, why? Yeah. Why? I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I was like, I I mean lately we used to sing, you see. We used to sing, but it used to help us out, you see.
Did you have any special numbers to sing?

Well, most of them. Anything, huh? Yes, more than a number to sing. Somebody get a new piece like that, the girls want to definitely get a piano carpet. We get them piano carpets. That's why I used to go and buy them piano carpets. When they want a new song, they give it to me, I'll go buy the piano carpet, and I'll play the chorus. That's all. I never did, I never did make the introduction, no music them times, only the chorus. Now when I get music from Lil Feastin them, you got the introduction to play, you understand? So they cut that out. They play the first, and then stay on the chorus all the time. But most now they just play the chorus, them times. Yeah, play the chorus once, and then play the chorus all the time.
Well I like introduction, verse, and chorus myself. Yeah. I like to hear it all.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Well verse, and then you just make the introduction. Only when you get with the big string bands, you might make a introduction. Then you play the chorus, then you go in the chorus.
Did you ever hear of Scott Joplin? Scott Joplin? He was, it wasn't from here, but he wrote music.

Oh, these are them Scott Joplin books, them red books? Yeah. Well I bought four of them. Yeah? Chris Kelly got the cornet book and he died, and I never did got it the most. Yeah, did you? I wrote it to him, I never did got my cornet. I got the violin part down in the locker there somewhere. Yeah, the violin part. But in them parts they had no saxophone then, you understand? Well they had the trombone part, the violin, cornet, I bought four books. The only four of them I see was trombone, trombone, violin, clarinet.
Well what did Chris Kelly play? The cornet.
And you gave me a book then?
Yeah, I wrote it in my book.
Well that would be the fourth one then.
Eh?
That would be the fourth one then.
Cornet, clarinet, trombone, and violin, yeah. Yeah, well that's what I wanted to do. That makes four.
Boy, that's what I had. That's right. I wrote it in my book when they had the market here on the right behind the auditorium there. Trim A. Trim A.
It had the market there a long time.

I wrote it in my book then, nobody just got my book. They died and nobody just got my book. They died and nobody just got my book. They died and nobody just got my book. And so I got to go to read book, I think it was Lucey I learned the book to, but I kept the violin book. It's down there in the locker there now. Yeah. That's got, well that was hard. I said that's the only boy used to play, I had a piece from Scott Joplin, that book, they called it, what's the name of that, what's his name, Israel Garman, is the only fellow who played that piece that played that piece, is Frog Leg I think it's called. Oh yeah, that's nice. Yeah, Frog Leg. And they had another piece there, the fellas couldn't play it because it's in five shops. In five shops, and Israel is the only one who could play, is the Garman. Was it harder than African Pass?
African Pass, well that was easy.
That was easy. Yeah, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. That's the only boy I could play. I tried him there in lunches out with Jack Carey. And I tried him out. He's the only one who could play that piece.
But they played afterwards. They learned later. They learned later afterwards, yeah. I like Kinklitz and I like what's his name, Minstrel Man. Minstrel Man, yeah.
All that's good. And they had mazookas in there too, you know. The waltzes, the Scott Joplin.
The Ragtime Dance, do you remember that?
The Ragtime Dance.
That was good.
Yeah, Ragtime Dance. He had to play that.
I got the words to that.
Yeah? Yeah, Ragtime Dance. Yeah, I used to play all that stuff. But that's the hardest music we had, the Scott Joplin. Them red books.
Mm-hmm.
Will you play?
What were you saying there now? Let's get it down on the tape.
What?
You were saying about the bands, the white ragtime bands.

Yeah, they didn't have them when I was playing up there. They hadn't many. We all, all the colored, you were all the colored bands. You understand? They didn't have no white bands. You wouldn't hire them.
I thought you said they had one just then, huh?
I had one. That's a brass band. A brass band? A brass band. Out the lake. Millen Breaks. Played out there every Sunday evening.
And they played ragtime?
Well, they was a regular big band. They were red, huh? Yeah. I see. That's the only white band they had in town.
Did you know that Reliance band? That's the white band? Who?
The Reliance band. The Reliance band.
Jack Lane had it.
Jack Lane. Papa Lane had it going?
Yeah. He used to use Shield Barquet and Dave Perkins, you know? Yeah, yeah. You know how they get the blomps, you know?
Yeah, I know. Used to change up there, Dave Perkins. Yeah, all of the different guys. Dave Perkins, he used to play tramo with them. Yeah.
You understand? Mattaya played with them.
Yeah.
Oh no.
And Joyce Barquet used to play with them, too. And this fellow, Nau, he was very light too, you know? Manetta sample?
Manetta sample?

He used to play with them some time. Yeah. I'm talking about the big band, the brass band, I'm talking about in the street. Oh yeah. But in them times they didn't have no many bands, white bands then. He used to play with them, you know, cut. Now, this boy there would play bass now, what do you call it? Let's call his name, change, let's call his name.
Oh, it's drag? Drag. Okay.

And see, the time when I was going at the lake, I used to have six pieces. But they used to have three pieces of drag. I never just played with him. But we didn't, you know, we didn't, he would play with them just with the little fellas, Willie Phillip and all them different fellas.
Who's Willie Phillip?
He's a guy, he's a fella used to play corny with drag.
Was he a reader or head man or what?

No, he was head, yeah he's a head man. Yeah, all. Yeah. You know, just know them how they read music. But Poissy and his brother. Now, them fellas there used to be, now all, most of all Jack Carey, band always, break time. All by the people, so. Louie, Louie Nelson. Did you ever hear this name? Yeah, I heard him. Yeah? He wasn't reading then. No. Never did read, huh?
No, no. Never did read, huh? No, no, never did read. And there were, the fella playing the trombone, what do you call them again, from Al Jays.

Frankie Dutton. Mm-hm. They never did read. Buddy Dutton. Buddy Dutton. But he read. Yeah, you know Yank's dear brother. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. But he read, he read musicals. He used to play that band over the roof before Allen. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. because he used to play that band over the roof, before Allen made up his band.
That's Joel Lazard you're talking about? Joel Lazard, that's right.
Joel Lazard.
Well, who was in Joel Lazard's band?
